title: Rents, Wages and the Missing Middle
standfirst: Where the money goes for people on average pay.
body: Ask someone on an ordinary salary where their money goes and the answer usually starts with housing. For many people in their twenties and thirties, rent is now the single largest bill, by a long way.

A useful rule of thumb is that housing should take no more than about a third of take-home pay. In much of the country, renters on average wages are well past that line. Once rent, bills and transport are paid, the amount left for everything else is thin.
This is the missing middle: people who earn too much for most help, but not enough to save, buy a home or absorb a shock. A broken boiler or a car repair can undo months of careful budgeting.

The simple answer is that demand has grown faster than supply for decades. Britain has not built enough homes where people want to live, and the homes that are built tend to be expensive. Rising interest rates have added pressure, as some landlords pass higher mortgage costs on to tenants.

More homes, built faster, is the long-term answer that nearly everyone agrees on and few governments deliver. In the shorter term, the debate is about planning rules, the tax treatment of landlords, and support for first-time buyers.

For the missing middle, the stakes are high. A generation that cannot save cannot build security, and a country where work does not pay for a home will struggle to persuade people that effort is rewarded.
